name: review-flight-deck
title: A reviewer surface above several pull requests
outcome: On every pull request change, the flightdeck simulates possible paths to close the whole open set, replays the best one or two with real git, and shows the reviewer one validated path. The reviewer reads what they would have when it is done, then what each pull request adds, then whether the merges hold.
done_when: A pull request event starts the mode without a person naming a set.
A pull request with no description gets one from /pr:generate before the flightdeck reads it.
The set the reviewer sees excludes whatever the team's own auto-merge rules already handled.
Every simulation runs against the common ancestor of the open branches, never against the default branch as it stands today.
The mode simulates at least three paths, then replays the best one or two with real git and counts the conflicts.
The front page leads with the state the reviewer would have if they accept, not with the mechanics of getting there.
The path names each pull request and what it contributes, in the order the pull requests can land.
The mergeability chain is shown as its own evidence, separate from the outcome and separate from the path.
The alternatives are visible on the front page and reachable only from inside the recommendation.
Each alternative states the reason it lost, and a git-replayed reason where one exists.
The recommendation names what the replay could not check.
The reviewer acts on a pass from the page, and each action appends one ledger line.
The reviewer opens any pull request in the existing four-level layout, and returns.
The viewer renders the paths and computes none of them.
A pull request the path cannot carry is shown on the front page, not buried, with the kind of block named: superseded, or a conflict a merge cannot resolve.
A blocked pull request carries the file and the line span, what each side did, and two or three ways out with one recommended.
The outcome states what the reviewer would not have, alongside what they would.
The reviewer commits to a path once, and then chooses the pace: all bundles in one run, or one bundle with a checkpoint after each.
No bundle merges onto the default branch. Each merges onto its own integration branch, and the default branch sees one pull request at the end.
Accepting a path records it. A runner performs it, and the page says so.
abort_if: The stop count for a set is not materially lower than the total number of authored files the pull requests change. Measured over 27 pairs of merged pull requests in this bundle, the ratio runs from 0.00 to 0.41, and every pair reduces. This criterion is met for the whole corpus.

Superseded criterion, kept for the record: the first version of this test compared the stop count against the shared-file list, not against the total changed files. That was the wrong baseline, because a reviewer's alternative is reading both diffs in full, not reading the shared subset. On that wrong baseline only 9 of 27 pairs reduce, and pull requests 11 and 12 give 37 stops against 22 shared files.
A proposed partition anchors reviewers more than it helps them, measured against a set they also reviewed without one.

A simulation run against the default branch instead of the common ancestor. It inverts the order whenever an open pull request restructures the tree, and it produces a confident wrong answer rather than no answer.

min_work.derived_from: 3 districts touched (viewer, scripts, .cobuilder-architect). 4 colliding ADRs: ADR-0001 (one self-contained file under a blocking content policy), ADR-0018 (one lifecycle surface and a derived record index), ADR-0019 (the append-only ledger, with its vocabulary fixed at comment, reply, and state), ADR-0020 (viewer parts and an author-time build, decided and not executed). 1 boundary rule crossed: no plugin names another plugin's path, so the viewer reaches the proposal through the bundle.
min_work.note: Stage 3 issued six isolated exploration frames and one separate critic pass. Stage 4 raised three challenges and the engineer answered all three. The engineer overruled the recommended approach and chose the Braid and the Cut together, on the ground that both do work on the reviewer's behalf before the reviewer arrives. That choice replaced the stated approach and moved the whole computation terminal-side, which also removed the ledger write-path defect the first challenge raised. Stage 7 asked whether this is one pull request or several. The engineer chose one, so every epic carries the same branch, design/review-flight-deck, and the six epics are units of work inside one review rather than six pull requests. A scratchpad run of E1's arithmetic over the cached diffs corrected the first abort criterion, which compared stops against shared files rather than against total changed files. Round 2: the engineer revised the intent. The mode is named flightdeck. It runs on a pull request event, not on a named set, and it offers several proposals rather than one partition. Each proposal carries a narrative and a diagram. The six epics collapse into four. ADR-0022's boundary holds unchanged. Automatic triggering collides with the no-hooks install rule and is the one open decision. Round 3: the engineer resolved the trigger themselves, with a scheduled skill run or a workflow, and it stops being an open question. The remaining work is the layout and the proposal quality. flightdeck-prototype.html is the layout, close to working: three views, the actions a reviewer takes from the page, a drill-in to the existing four-level layout, and an append-only ledger. Round 4: the engineer set the presentation rules. Show one recommendation, not three. Keep the alternatives visible and unreachable until the reviewer opens the recommendation. Write the story of what would happen, not the structure of the options. Work at the scale of every open pull request, and drop whatever the team's auto-merge already handled. The pipeline becomes simulate from records, then a git what-if on the top one or two, then a validated recommendation. Precomputing mergeable git slices may exist elsewhere, and the narrative plus the options is the part that does not. Round 5: the engineer found a real error. The first recommendation simulated against master as it stands today, which already carries the five-plugin split, so it put the restructure first and the earlier work last. With all seventeen pull requests open the base is 0c099be, where commands/, scripts/ and skills/ still exist, and six open pull requests write into exactly those three directories that pull request 11 deletes. The correct order is the reverse of what I proposed. Two more corrections. The language must state the outcome first and then each pull request's contribution, never the mechanics. And the product is a set of possible paths to close the whole open set, which separates into three things: whether the merges physically hold, what the reviewer ends up with, and the proposed order. Round 6: three additions and one correction. A path never carries every open pull request, so the layout surfaces the ones it cannot: a superseded branch and a branch with a conflict a merge cannot resolve. Both appear on the front page with a way out, because a hard conflict needs a person and not a retry. The outcome states what the reviewer would not have, next to what they would. The reviewer commits to a path once and then controls the pace, one bundle at a time by default, with a checkpoint tree they can check out between bundles. And nothing merges onto the default branch: each bundle merges onto its own integration branch, so abandoning a path is three branch deletions. The page no longer says nothing reaches GitHub. It records the decision, and a runner performs it.

epics.outcome: A pull request with no description gets one from /pr:generate before the flightdeck reads it. A pull request that already has one is left alone.
epics.note: New in round 4. It closes the gap the prototype had to show as a warning: 8 of 12 pull requests in this repository carry no intent block. Reuses generate mode whole, and adds only the check for an existing description.

epics.outcome: The mode lists every open pull request with its head branch, changed files, and design, and marks the ones the team's auto-merge rules already handled.
epics.note: The same work as the first epic of the inflight-record-store design. Build it once, in shared code. The auto-merge split is read from the team's own rules, and this design does not define them.

epics.outcome: The mode simulates at least three paths to close the whole open set, each against the common ancestor of the open branches, and each naming an order with the evidence for it.
epics.note: divergent-exploration.md already generates competing options in isolation and criticises them in a separate pass. The baseline is load-bearing: simulating against the default branch inverts the order whenever an open pull request restructures the tree.

epics.outcome: The mode replays the best one or two paths on a scratch worktree from the common ancestor, counts the real conflicts, and promotes the survivor. The mergeability chain it produces is shown to the reviewer as evidence in its own right.
epics.note: New in round 4, and the step that makes the recommendation something to stand behind. Read-only against a scratch worktree. A route that fails the replay is kept, with the failure as its reason for losing. Systems that precompute mergeable slices may already do this part, so keep the interface narrow enough to swap one in. It must also classify what it cannot merge. A superseded branch and an unresolvable conflict are different findings and get different treatments in the layout.

epics.outcome: Each path carries the state the reviewer would have when it is done, and one line per pull request saying what that pull request contributes. A losing path carries the reason it lost.
epics.note: Round 5 fixed the register. State the outcome first, then the contributions, and never lead with the mechanics. The engineer's worked example: perform the renames and restructuring across the repository, which merges without conflict, then incorporate the new viewer into the resulting structure and naming conventions.

epics.outcome: The front page shows one recommendation and an unreachable marker for the alternatives. Opening the recommendation unlocks them. The reviewer acts on a wave from the page, and each action appends one ledger line.
epics.note: Reuses the existing view modes, the level rail, and the ledger from ADR-0019. flightdeck-prototype.html is the reference layout.

epics.outcome: A runner reads an accepted path from the ledger and merges each bundle onto its own integration branch, never onto the default branch. It stops at a checkpoint between bundles when the reviewer chose one bundle at a time.
epics.note: New in round 6, and the first epic in this design that writes to a remote. The integration branch per bundle is what makes a path abandonable: delete three branches and the default branch never saw any of it. The default branch receives one pull request, from the last bundle's branch.
